## 4. Movies about everyday life in American cities around the 1840s–1850s? Not Westerns

**Score:** 19
**Body:** I'm looking for movies set in American cities around the 1840s–1850s, especially ones that show what everyday urban life was actually like: streets, houses, shops, offices, taverns, transportation, social life, different classes, etc.

I'm Italian, and I've realized something funny: thanks to movies I've probably seen a hundred versions of what life was like for cowboys, settlers and people on the frontier, but I know surprisingly little about how an ordinary person lived in New York, Boston, Philadelphia, Baltimore or other American cities in the same period.

I'm not necessarily looking for movies *about* major historical events. In fact, I'd be especially interested in films where the city and normal daily life are a big part of the setting.

Something around 1840–1860 would be ideal, but I'm happy to go a little earlier or later if the atmosphere is similar.

I've already thought of *Gangs of New York*, although that's obviously a rather extreme side of urban life.

Any recommendations?

### Top 8 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Gangs of New York is set in exactly this time frame.
  - I think that’s what I like most about this movie, the setting. 
2. It’s a setting I’d like to see more of in films.  Sadly underrepresented.
  - Yeah, I'm definitely no expert, but I think 90% of American films set in the US during that period are Westerns?
3. Washington Square (book & film)
4. First thing that comes to mind is all the various adaptations of *Little Women*, which show daily life in Concord and Boston (and later, New York City) throughout the 1860s.

If you don't mind watching older films, there was a big burst of high-budget period pieces about the late 18th century in the late 1930s.

*In Old Chicago* is one of my favorites, a Zanuck-era movie about the O'Leary family in Chicago in the years leading up to the Great Chicago Fire of 1871. It might be the most relevant to your interests since it really gets into city scenes, showing people starting a business and working with their neighbors, etc.

*The Toast of New York* is about some of the robber barons and Wall Street hotshots of the 1860s. If I recall correctly, it's mostly set in boardrooms and drawing rooms, but it's still clearly NYC of the 1860s.
5. These are still rural America but not westerns:

* Tom Sawyer
* Huck Finn
* Our Hospitality (1923) with Buster Keaton
* The Emigrants (1971)/The New Land (1972)
* Young Mr. Lincoln
* The Flame of New Orleans
* Reap the Wild Wind
* The Raven (2012)

you might also ask at r/PeriodDramas 
6. Set in 1880s and a series but sounds like “The Guilded Age” might be for you. Set mainly in NYC
  - I also thought of The Gilded Age. Such an excellent show, and does a great job of showing urban life of late 19th century America. 

I’ve read and written a lot about the time period OP is interested in. There’s such a rich literature in terms of history, biography, and novels about the 1840s and 50s, but just so few films that aren’t westerns or war films. (I happened to think of The Good Lord Bird, a Showtime miniseries that was well made and an adaptation of the novel, but it was at heart a political thriller mostly set in Kansas, following the life of the abolitionist John Brown. I highly recommend it, but not what OP is looking for.)
7. Meet Me In St Louis

## 3. Resident Evil (2026) ending explained, thematically

**Score:** 136
**Body:** ***Resident Evil*** ends with a mutated Bryan roaring at the National Guard helicopters. It seems like a bad ending, as our protagonist has become a terrifying monstrosity. But there’s actually a lot more going on. 

At the start of ***Resident Evil***, Bryan’s in the middle of a conversation with his girlfriend, Michelle. She’s told him she’s pregnant and he has a pretty standard response: fear. Because he’s afraid of his life changing, he hems and haws about what to do. 

Zach Cregger starts this way because he wants the audience to know, up front, that the entire movie is an externalization of the internal chaos going on inside of Bryan. That’s why he spends the entire movie “carrying” the green bag, and we even have the dialogue where he tells Michelle that “this is life that I’m carrying, right now.” 

[Full explanation](https://filmcolossus.com/resident-evil-ending-explained/)

3. For me, the ending shows the tragedy of the Raccoon City people. He turns into a monster similar to the one chasing him, but we only see it as a threat to our protagonist. In the ending, as he becomes one of them, we feel for him, showing that every monster we face has a story and fell victim to the corporation's tragedy
4. I felt sooo bad for him. 
  - First thing I said to my wife when the movie ended was that it was huge gut punch to give us such a likeable character and then not even let him die, but instead turn into a monster who's probably still aware on some level of what's happening to him...
5. Ending was great. Would’ve been anticlimactic otherwise 
6. Are people forgetting that Umbrella scientists are the FUCKING WORST in terms of self awareness and morality. There's a million memes about the logs they have lmao. I loved the main character, he carried the movie, but as soon as he walked in that lab I knew ALL of them were cooked

## 5. Why prisoners still feels so uncomfortable to watch

**Score:** 123
**Body:** Prisoners is one of those movies where the tension comes less from what happens and more from the choices people make when they feel they have no other options.

What I find interesting is how the movie keeps blurring the line between justice and obsession. You can understand why the characters act the way they do while still questioning how far they're willing to go.

The atmosphere also makes everything feel heavier, especially  with the cinematography and constant sense of uncertainty.

For those who have seen it, what do you think the movie is ultimately saying about justice and revenge?





### Top 7 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. To me this is still one of the best films of this century, I almost didn't want to blink throughout the runtime.
2. This film touches directly and relentlessly on a deep and dangerous pressure point in American culture: the desire to utterly destroy the right (bad) people and the perverse appeal of participating directly in that destruction. This American cultural pathology has gotten much worse since the release of the film.
3. ![gif](giphy|pV0lVLeA0JXjBiO5Cp)
4. Not more about Justice & Revenge but more like it showed how far a man would go when it comes to his family & the drain that comes on him as well. Like one of the things that really drew me into the film was how you see Hugh Jackman's character slowly lose himself as he gets more desperate but at the same time also constantly doubt himself if whether he is doing the right thing to get his daughter back. 
  - Yeah, exactly. That slow loss of himself is what makes his character so compelling. You can understand why he keeps pushing forward while also watching him question how far he's willing to go. That desperation really makes the movie hit harder.
5. I think it has a lot to do with visual language and use of sound by Denis. He does this in every film, Incendies, Arrival.  
Slow place with a gradual buildup, still frames, longer shots, letting us stay and observe the actors expressions and the environment.  
He doesn’t over use music. The silence creeps on us. Even in the hammer scene “where is my daughter” there is not much music and the loud bangs shock you.
  - Yes! One of my gripes with modern films is that they over use music to tell you how to feel, as opposed to the acting and actual scene going on. 
6. Hugh Jackman is fascinating in this. This was an absolute epic performance that somehow went under the radar until streaming. If he cranked out a few more movies like this, he’d be mentioned alongside Daniel Day Lewis and other all-time actors.
  - Same with Gyllenhaal. Dude was captivating as Det. Loki.
    - Oh no doubt. I only said that about Jackman because he’s not always on the list of the “greatest actors today.” Gyllenhall is often rated pretty highly. But they were powerhouses in this film.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. Why A.I. Artificial Intelligence is on my list of "10 Favorite Films"....

**Score:** 27
**Body:** The film AI Artificial Intelligence is one of my favorite films. I find it challenging, mystifying, compelling, ambitious, and emotionally rewarding. It presents so many questions without presuming to having the answers, while acting almost as a frightening prophecy about the future of mankind. When it begins, it seems sure of the idea that robots can never reach the same level of consciousness as humans, but by the end, it doesn't seem so sure. It tells the story of a fundamentally "unreal" boy who will stop at nothing to become real for the sole purpose of finally earning his mother's love. One could argue that it is merely his programming that compels him to do so, and that such compulsions don't equate to genuine consciousness. But don't we ourselves operate under similar programmings? Programmings whose original causes are mysterious, and ones that endlessly compel us to earn the love of others? That seems to be the questions the film is asking. By the end of the film, David paradoxically seems like the most human character in the entire film and we rejoice in his ability to beat the odds to reach his heart's desire, in spite of all the inhuman ways in which he was treated. He uses the story of Pinnochio, much like we create stories to make sense of our lives, and in doing so, makes his life meaningful to himself and others. What could be more human than that?

### Top 4 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. It was the only movie where I actually cried from anguish and sadness. What triggered me was the absolute cruelty of discovering your subjective experience is a fake construct, your feelings are a simulation and the sub product of a cold machinery with "higher purposes" beyond human connection.

All these realizations, that came too me at 16 years old because the movie was that great at making you see the horror in the "virtualization of human connection", stuck with me forever and left a lingering impression. Easily one of my favourite films as well.
  - My mom passed when I was a baby and when I was a kid I used to wish on a star that she would come back to life... Lol. So this movie makes me fucking weep at the end haha
  - Don't worry pal, I cried profusely as well. My Mom had recently passed when I first watched it, and this film unexpectedly became a very healing (albeit melancholic) experience for me. Apparently we're not alone, as even British Arthouse Filmmaker Ken Russell (Director of the most X rated films of the 20th Century) wept like a baby as he watched the ending. It's definitely poignant. 
2. The opening ~45 minutes are fascinating in themselves especially in today’s age, given that it’s about a human emotionally enmeshing with an AI, something that’s started happening now with chatbots, with kinda scary results. And the movie doesn’t shy away from the scary aspects too. 

Some bits in the middle are a bit weird tonally, but there are some amazing moments too. And the final act is pretty cool and imaginative.

It’s uneven IMO but the parts that land are really inspired. I suspect it will age well and be looked upon fondly given the current rise of AI and the questions raised by that
  - You know, people often complain about tonal inconsistencies, but to me that's part of what makes the movie so interesting. That it's both a Pinocchio retelling and an actually very bleak dystopian future at the same time. For me, that's a feature, not a bug.
3. This movie is divisive! My wife hates it but she’s only seen it once. I’ve seen it a few times and enjoy it more each time.

The ending is a bit of a misdirection with far more uncomfortable implications under the surface. Here, Spielberg’s sentimentality feels more like artifice than technique. 
  - >The ending is a bit of a misdirection with far more uncomfortable implications under the surface. Here, Spielberg’s sentimentality feels more like artifice than technique.

For what it's worth, the late screenwriter Ian Watson has described that ending as faithful to Kubrick's original vision.

As you suggest, the "uncomfortable implications" are very intentional, and what makes it interesting is that you can read it as both a sentimental heartwarming ending AND a really tragic, disturbing ending.
4. I love the movie AI. I saw it in the theaters, mostly because it was Stanley Kubrick's baby, and I loved it - it truly is the final Kubrick film IMO. I watched it again recently, and was even more moved by it than when it was new. Such a remarkable movie. On the one hand I can sort of see why people don't like it - much as many people wouldn't enjoy Barry Lyndon or Paths of Glory - but on the other hand I don't know how you can't see the amazing artistry involved in so many aspects of the movie.

Not to mention Jude Law is something else in his supporting role. And that ending! What an emotional roller coaster.

## 2. Robert Altman Video Essay

**Score:** 17
**Body:** Hi everybody! I made a video essay about Robert Altman and how he created his unique style of filmmaking and implemented it throughout the years. I'm a huge Altman fan and I've always felt like his documentary style approach to narrative is a true expansion of the medium. Check it out and let me know what you think!

  
[https://youtu.be/t3xzQkJbfCw?si=aAu0398FisOYoSfW](https://youtu.be/t3xzQkJbfCw?si=aAu0398FisOYoSfW)

### Top 1 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I'll check this out this afternoon thanks for the recc. I'm always waiting for someone to come along and work off of Altman's vision - Kristin Thompson described them as "network narrative" films rather than "ensemble", where the movie itself is the collection of set pieces the characters interact in but their stories are dissonant but ultimately commenting on the same subject and crossing over in a satisfying way. It's extremely high level writing, possibly *the* highest level of writing (to me) in terms of realizing a movie that is both about a subject and about its characters - an aspirational idea that certain people have definitely come close to but no one has surpassed since the release of Short Cuts.
  - I would say that Magnolia, which is very much influenced by Short Cuts, is the closest you'll get to that. 
    - I agree that's the closest someone has come - sadly, to avoid being pigeonholed, PTA made a hard pivot after that towards protag-centrality, assumedly having seen the way Tarantino was catalogued as a reference-maker and not wanting to be boxed in as "Altman 2". Technically i think the last movie to attempt it would have been "Love Actually" and all its holiday themed follow ups, I can't think of a more recent attempt. Too expensive I guess! And who wants to sign on without the possibility of a leading role?

## 3. How long did it take for you to feel like you understand movies?

**Score:** 12
**Body:** I've had a lifelong passion for the arts and storytelling, and as of late, I've really been trying to watch all the movies I can and watch some again and again so I can really get a grasp of the language cast and crew use to make a movie. I've even started keeping a journal so I can make observations, comparisons, and other notes to really make sense of it all.

It's only been about half a year since I've really started to sink my teeth in, but I can't help but be discouraged when there are movies (especially popular ones) that I don't really "get".

  
Just as an example, recently, I saw *Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma*, and while it was obviously well made, the subtext (and even plenty of the text) was indecipherable to me, and that sucked because I really wanted to like it.

  
So TL;DR, how long did it take for you to become familiar enough with the language of cinema to the point you felt like you could consistently make an informed opinion? (keyword: informed).

EDIT: I want to thank everyone so very much for being understanding and encouraging avenues for me to explore and to come to my own conclusions!

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Idk if there is a discrete time at which you become a “movie-understander”. Some movies you will get and some you will not. It entirely depends on your taste, your knowledge of the subject matter, and your mindset as you are experiencing the thing.

*Camp Miasma* is an interesting one. People have taken a lot of different things away from it, some which are entirely opposed to one another.

I happen to have studied Lacanian Psychoanalysis when I was young, so I picked up a lot on those themes which were very, very present in the movie. I would be shocked if most people were able to pick those up. That is not for a lack of being able to understand, but because it would take you spending the time to read that stuff. In no way is it general knowledge.
2. I mean, Teenage Sex & Death is pretty deep into film theory, drawing on feminist readings of slasher films. So I wouldn’t beat yourself up over that one. 

What type of insight are you hoping to achieve? Is it the way film technique influences readings, ie—the importance of editing, lighting, etc? Or is it more understanding subtext etc? 

If it’s the latter, you could tackle something big and easy. How 80s action movies reflect American foreign policy, or the way the Tony Stark/Capt America relationship reflects 00s and 10s tensions between moderate republicans and democrats.

Remember that there’s a difference between actually “not knowing what’s going on” and not understanding why a movie is choosing to depict what’s going on in a certain way.

*Camp Miasma* is a great example of this: the movie is a very personal one to Schoenbrun and makes a bunch of “weird” and intuitive choices. But really the primary ideas are pretty simple and explicit ones that the two main characters discuss directly in straightforward scenes that aren’t abstract or interpretive at all. The movie’s about the things it seems to be about: orgasms and old horror movies. There are various ways you can think about the movie’s “subtext,” but for the movie to actually be *decipherable*, you don’t actually need to go any deeper than following the conversations Einbinder and Anderson’s character has (which are supplemented, if you like, by music and artistic imagery).
